title: Clozapine: monitoring and red flags
blurb: Follow the clozapine blood-test schedule and act fast on infection, tachycardia, constipation, smoking changes and missed doses.
question: Dele, 34, started clozapine five weeks ago for treatment-resistant schizophrenia. He tells the nurse he has a sore throat and feels shivery; his temperature is 38.3 C. What is the most appropriate action?

teach.body: Clozapine is the antipsychotic NICE recommends for schizophrenia that has not responded to adequate trials of at least two antipsychotics, at least one a non-clozapine second-generation drug. It works when others have failed, but it can cause neutropenia and agranulocytosis, myocarditis, severe constipation and seizures. In plain English: it is the most effective option for resistant illness and the one that needs the closest watching. The nurse's job is to keep the blood tests on time and spot the red flags early.

Clozapine can suppress white cells. Blood results go through a clozapine patient monitoring service, and clozapine is stopped permanently if the white cell count falls below 3000/mm3 or the absolute neutrophil count below 1500/mm3. Because counts can fall between tests, people must report any sign of infection straight away: sore throat, fever or a flu-like illness. The response is an urgent full blood count and prescriber review, not simply paracetamol.

teach.caption: Sources: BNF clozapine; MHRA 2017 (constipation) and 2020 (smoking).

teach.body: Fatal myocarditis and cardiomyopathy are reported, most commonly in the first 2 months. Persistent tachycardia, especially early on, should prompt checks; if myocarditis is suspected clozapine is stopped and a cardiologist reviews urgently, and it is never restarted. Clozapine also slows the gut: constipation can progress to faecal impaction and paralytic ileus. The MHRA advises patients to seek medical advice before taking the next dose if constipation develops.
teach.cite: BNF clozapine; MHRA Drug Safety Update Oct 2017

steps.label: Stops smoking
steps.sub: Admission to a smoke-free ward, quitting, or switch to e-cigarette

root.label: Doses missed
root.sub: Check how long since the last dose

children.label: Do not give usual dose
children.sub: Re-titrate from 12.5 mg on prescriber's plan

teach.caption: Restarting the full dose after a gap risks hypotension, collapse and respiratory or cardiac arrest (BNF).

teach.body: Staff Nurse Patel on the acute ward notes Dele is in week 5, inside the weekly-test period, with fever and a sore throat. She treats this as possible neutropenia: she informs the prescriber at once, arranges an urgent full blood count and holds the next dose pending advice. She also checks his pulse for tachycardia, asks about bowels and records everything. Paracetamol alone, or waiting for the routine weekly test, could miss agranulocytosis.

teach.text: Hypersalivation (drooling, especially at night) is common and expected with clozapine; fever with a sore throat is the red flag. And remember the direction: stopping smoking RAISES clozapine levels. Many candidates reverse it.

items: FBC weekly for 18 weeks, at least fortnightly to 1 year, then at least 4-weekly.
Stop if WBC below 3000/mm3 or ANC below 1500/mm3; infection signs need an urgent FBC.
Persistent tachycardia in the first 2 months: think myocarditis, stop and get urgent review.
Constipation can be fatal: seek advice before the next dose.
Stopping smoking raises levels; more than 48 hours missed means re-titration.

summary: You can now follow the clozapine blood-test schedule and recognise neutropenia, myocarditis, constipation and toxicity. You know what to do when a person stops smoking or misses doses.

A.q: How often is a full blood count needed during the first 18 weeks of clozapine treatment?
options: Every two weeks
Every four weeks
Weekly
Every three months
A.why: BNF: leucocyte and differential counts weekly for 18 weeks, then at least every 2 weeks until 1 year, then at least every 4 weeks.

whyNot.0: Fortnightly testing applies from week 18 to 1 year.
whyNot.1: Four-weekly testing applies after the first year.
whyNot.3: Three-monthly is a lithium schedule, not a clozapine one.

A.q: When is clozapine-induced myocarditis most commonly seen?
options: After the first year of treatment
In the first 2 months of treatment
In the first 2 days after a dose rise
In the month after clozapine is stopped
A.why: BNF: fatal myocarditis is reported most commonly in the first 2 months, so persistent tachycardia early in treatment needs checking.

whyNot.0: Cardiomyopathy can occur later, but myocarditis clusters in the first 2 months.
whyNot.2: The recognised peak is the first 2 months of treatment, not days after a dose change.
whyNot.3: Myocarditis is linked to the early weeks of taking clozapine, not to stopping it.

A.q: What should a person taking clozapine be told to do if they become constipated?
options: Seek medical advice before the next dose
Halve the next dose until the bowels open
Increase fluids and review after 7 days
Buy an over-the-counter laxative and carry on
A.why: MHRA (2017): constipation with clozapine can progress to obstruction, impaction and paralytic ileus, including fatal cases; patients should seek medical advice before taking the next dose.

whyNot.1: Self-adjusting the dose is unsafe and does not get the bowel assessed.
whyNot.2: Waiting a week risks ileus developing unnoticed.
whyNot.3: Self-treating without review can miss a developing obstruction.

B.q: Grace, 41, is admitted to a smoke-free ward. She smoked 30 cigarettes a day and takes clozapine. Four days later she is unusually drowsy and drooling more. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Reassure her that sedation is a common side effect
Ask the prescriber to raise the dose to cover the change
Tell the prescriber and request a clozapine blood level
Suggest short escorted breaks so she can smoke outside
B.why: MHRA (2020): smoking induces clozapine metabolism, so stopping raises levels and toxicity risk. Report it and request a level so the dose can be reviewed.

whyNot.0: New drowsiness after stopping smoking suggests rising levels, which need review.
whyNot.1: Levels rise when smoking stops, so a higher dose would worsen toxicity.
whyNot.3: Restarting smoking is not the safe answer; levels are managed by monitoring and dose review.

B.q: Tomasz, 29, returns to the ward after going missing for three days without his clozapine. The usual evening dose is due. What should the nurse do?
options: Give the usual evening dose as charted
Give a double dose to restore the level
Give half the usual dose and review tomorrow
Withhold it and ask for a re-titration plan
B.why: BNF: if more than 48 hours have passed since the last dose, clozapine is restarted at 12.5 mg and titrated again, so the nurse withholds the usual dose and contacts the prescriber.

whyNot.0: Restarting at the full dose after over 48 hours risks hypotension and collapse.
whyNot.1: Doubling is dangerous; after a gap of more than 48 hours clozapine is re-titrated from 12.5 mg, not caught up.
whyNot.2: Nurses do not improvise a dose; re-titration from 12.5 mg is prescribed.

B.q: Which finding in a person taking clozapine is expected and does NOT by itself need urgent escalation?
options: A temperature of 38.5 C with a sore throat
Drooling onto the pillow at night
Persistent resting pulse of 125 in week 3
No bowel movement for five days
B.why: Hypersalivation is a common, expected side effect of clozapine; it is managed but is not an emergency. The other three are red flags.

whyNot.0: Fever with a sore throat may signal neutropenia and needs an urgent FBC.
whyNot.2: Persistent tachycardia in the first 2 months may signal myocarditis.
whyNot.3: Constipation with clozapine can progress to fatal ileus and needs review.

C.q: Ahmed, 27, is in week 6 of clozapine. He has a resting pulse of 128 on three readings, feels breathless and says his chest feels tight. His last FBC was normal. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Give PRN lorazepam for anxiety and recheck in an hour
Record it and repeat the pulse at the next weekly bloods
Advise cutting caffeine and recheck the pulse tomorrow
Withhold clozapine and get urgent medical review today
C.why: BNF: persistent tachycardia, especially in the first 2 months, with chest symptoms suggests myocarditis; clozapine is stopped and the person is evaluated urgently by a cardiologist.

whyNot.0: Treating it as anxiety delays assessment of possible myocarditis.
whyNot.1: A week's delay is unsafe with suspected myocarditis.
whyNot.2: Persistent tachycardia with chest tightness needs same-day review, not lifestyle advice.

C.q: Lucy, 38, has taken clozapine for 4 months. Her routine result shows an absolute neutrophil count of 1200/mm3. She feels well. What is the correct response?
options: Continue clozapine and repeat the count next week
Halve the dose and repeat the count in 3 days
Stop clozapine and tell the prescriber now
Continue and start antibiotics as a precaution
C.why: BNF: clozapine is discontinued permanently if the ANC falls below 1500/mm3. Feeling well does not change this; the prescriber and monitoring service must be told urgently.

whyNot.0: A count below 1500/mm3 means stopping, not routine retesting.
whyNot.1: Dose reduction is not the response to a count below the stop threshold.
whyNot.3: Antibiotics do not address the drug causing neutropenia.

C.q: Sam, 45, on clozapine for 2 years, mentions he has swapped cigarettes for an e-cigarette, has opened his bowels once in 6 days and has abdominal bloating. Which action should come first?
options: Get urgent medical review before the next dose
Book a clozapine level for his next routine clinic visit
Praise the switch and offer a stop-smoking leaflet
Give the usual dose with a stimulant laxative tonight
C.why: Both issues need action, but bloating with severe constipation may be ileus, which can be fatal; MHRA advises medical advice before the next dose. The e-cigarette switch also needs a level, but the bowel is the immediate danger.

whyNot.1: The level matters, but a routine booking misses the urgent bowel risk.
whyNot.2: Smoking support is good, but it does not address possible ileus.
whyNot.3: Giving the next dose before assessment risks worsening obstruction.

reteach.title: Four things clozapine can do
reteach.question: Which clozapine problems must a nurse never miss?

blocks.body: Think of four checks. Blood: infection signs mean an urgent FBC. Heart: persistent tachycardia in the first 2 months means possible myocarditis. Bowel: constipation needs advice before the next dose. Level: stopping smoking or missing more than 48 hours of doses changes how much drug is in the body.

blocks.text: Drooling is common and expected. A fever is not.

explain.body: Weekly FBC for 18 weeks, at least every 2 weeks to 1 year, then at least every 4 weeks, and 4 weeks after stopping. Stop permanently if WBC below 3000/mm3 or ANC below 1500/mm3.

test.q: Josef has taken clozapine for 8 months. How often should his full blood count be checked as a minimum?
options: Weekly
Every 2 weeks
Every 4 weeks
Every 6 months
test.why: After the first 18 weeks and until 1 year, counts are checked at least every 2 weeks (BNF).

whyNot.0: Weekly testing covers the first 18 weeks.
whyNot.3: Six-monthly is far too infrequent for clozapine.

explain.body: Most common in the first 2 months. Persistent tachycardia, chest pain, breathlessness or flu-like symptoms early in treatment need urgent checks. If suspected: stop clozapine, urgent cardiology review, never rechallenge.

test.q: A man had clozapine-induced myocarditis last year and has recovered. His psychosis has relapsed. What applies to clozapine now?
options: It may be restarted at a lower dose
It may be restarted with weekly ECGs
It may be restarted after 12 months
It should be permanently avoided
test.why: BNF: discontinue permanently in clozapine-induced myocarditis or cardiomyopathy; it is not restarted.

whyNot.0: Dose reduction does not make rechallenge safe after myocarditis.
whyNot.1: ECG monitoring does not permit rechallenge.
whyNot.2: Time elapsed does not change the permanent contraindication.

explain.body: Clozapine impairs gut movement. Constipation can progress to faecal impaction, obstruction and paralytic ileus, sometimes fatal. Ask about bowels at every contact and advise seeking help before the next dose.

test.q: Which routine nursing question best reduces the risk of clozapine-related ileus?
options: How many hours are you sleeping each night?
Have you noticed any drooling at night?
When did you last open your bowels?
Are you drinking more coffee than usual?
test.why: Asking about bowel habit at each contact lets constipation be found and treated before it progresses (MHRA 2017).

whyNot.0: Sleep is useful to know but does not detect bowel problems.
whyNot.1: Drooling is a common side effect, not an ileus warning.
whyNot.3: Caffeine intake does not screen for constipation.

explain.body: Tobacco smoke speeds clozapine breakdown. Stopping smoking, or switching to an e-cigarette, raises the level: monitor levels and review the dose. After more than 48 hours without clozapine, restart at 12.5 mg and re-titrate.

test.q: Why should a nurse report that a person on clozapine has stopped smoking?
options: The clozapine level may fall and relapse follow
The clozapine level may rise and cause toxicity
Nicotine withdrawal blocks clozapine absorption
The blood test schedule must restart from week 1
test.why: Smoking induces clozapine metabolism; when it stops, levels rise and toxicity can follow (MHRA 2020), so levels are checked.

whyNot.0: This reverses the effect: levels rise, not fall.
whyNot.2: The interaction is through metabolism, not absorption.
whyNot.3: Stopping smoking does not reset the FBC schedule.
